A record of failures with their limits kept clear

Did the program break? Did a route fail under certain conditions? Was something proved impossible within a model? Or did the test simply lack enough information?

Choose a kind of failure. Each leaves different next steps available. Keeping those limits clear can save another person from repeating the same mistake.

Choose a kind of failure. Read what it rules out and what it leaves open.

Words used here
no-go result
A proof that a proposed route cannot work under stated conditions. It does not rule out every differently stated route.
scope
The particular question, conditions and range to which a claim applies.
Read the fuller explanation

The negative-results ledger distinguishes a software defect, an obstruction under stated assumptions, an exact no-go result and a test that lacked identifying information. “It failed” is too small a description to tell the next person what remains possible.

Each admitted negative record names the claim, adequacy of the test, active domain, evidence, allowed inference and stronger inference refused. It also names what new datum or changed assumption could reopen the route.

Examine a refusal here as a research object. Keeping a failed promotion visible can protect a correct smaller result from being discarded with it. Truthful limits make the world larger by showing where a different question can begin.

Where this comes from: Failures and what could reopen a question

Scoped negative knowledge · explicit reopening conditions

A record of failures with their limits kept clear

Distinguishes a broken program, a failed route, a proof of impossibility under conditions, and a test with too little information. It also asks what could change the conclusion.

Read the full source note

Negative results and reopening ledger

Separates software defects, domain-dependent obstructions, no-go results and inadequate information. A negative result retains its exact claim, assumptions, evidence and cheapest reopening datum. A failed test does not justify an unrestricted impossibility claim.
